'''Dudley Howard Williams''' {{Post-nominals|FRS}} (25 May 1937 – 3 November 2010) was a British [[biochemist]] known for utilizing [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] (NMR) spectroscopy and [[mass spectrometry]] in the study of molecular structure, especially the antibiotic [[vancomycin]].<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.cam.ac.uk/news/professor-dudley-williams-scd-frs-1937-2010|title=Professor Dudley Williams ScD, FRS 1937 – 2010|date=15 November 2010|website=University of Cambridge}}</ref><ref name=roysoc>{{cite journal|last1=Sanders|first1=Jeremy&nbsp;K.&nbsp;M.|last2=Robinson|first2=Dame Carol&nbsp;V.|date=31 December 2017|title=Dudley Howard Williams. 25 May 1937 — 3 November 2010|journal=Biographical Memoirs of Fellows of the Royal Society|volume=63|pages=567–583|doi=10.1098/rsbm.2017.0009|doi-access=free}}</ref><ref>{{cite journal|last=Watts|first=Geoff|date=2011|title=Dudley Howard Williams|journal=The Lancet|volume=377|issue=9760|pages=120|doi=10.1016/S0140-6736(11)60010-X|s2cid=54389359 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

==Biography==
Dudley Howard Williams was born on 25 May 1937 in [[Farsley]], Yorkshire, the only child of Lawrence Williams, an engineers chief order clerk,<ref>1939 England and Wales Register</ref> and Evelyn (née Hudson). He attended [[Pudsey Grammar School]], from where he gained a place at the [[University of Leeds]]. He graduated in 1958 with a first-class BSc in Chemistry.<ref name=roysoc/>

Williams' research for a PhD was on the synthesis of Vitamin D and related compounds, under the supervision of [[Basil Lythgoe]], FRS at Leeds; his degree was awarded in 1961. That same year he was awarded a [[Fulbright Program|Fulbright Scholarship]] and moved to [[Stanford University]] to work with [[Carl Djerassi]] exploring the application of [[mass spectrometry]] (MS) in organic chemistry. He used the evenings to investigate the use of [[nuclear magnetic resonance]] (NMR) on a 100&nbsp;MHz instrument with Norman Bhacca at nearby [[Varian Associates]]. "In three stunningly productive years, he showed how mass spectrometry and NMR … could transform the way that organic chemists worked. His textbooks, reviews, research papers and lectures revolutionised organic chemistry over the following years".<ref>{{cite news|last=Sanders|first=Jeremey&nbsp;K.&nbsp;M.|title= Dudley Williams obituary: Pioneering scientist in the fight against MRSA|newspaper=The Guardian|url=https://www.theguardian.com/society/2010/nov/24/dudley-williams-obituary|date=24 November 2010|access-date=2 July 2023}}</ref>

In December 1962 Djerassi gave Williams three months' leave to go back to England to marry Lorna Patricia Phyllis (always known as Pat) Bedford, whom he had met at Leeds. She was a secretary in the Chemistry department. They married on 9 March 1963 and travelled to California, which they enjoyed exploring in their leisure time.

The next move was to Cambridge in 1964, to take up a junior position in Organic Chemistry, at the invitation of [[Alexander R. Todd|Lord Todd]]. A condition of the move was that the department should buy a Varian 100&nbsp;MHz NMR spectrometer and an AEI MS9 mass spectrometer. Williams stayed at Cambridge until his retirement in 2004.

In his memoir of Dudley Williams, Sanders noted that "the different areas of [his] science overlapped, intertwined and evolved so it is not easy to separate them out for discussion".<ref name=roysoc/>  He summarized Williams' work in three areas
*NMR and MS
{{block indent|em=1|1=A key contribution here was the use of shift reagents to alter NMR spectra to reveal more detail.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Sanders|first1=Jeremy&nbsp;K.&nbsp;M.|last2=Williams|first2=Dudley H|title=A shift reagent for use in nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy. A first-order spectrum of n-hexanol|journal=J. Chem. Soc. D|year=1970|issue=7 |pages=422–423|doi=10.1039/c29700000422 }}</ref>}}
{{block indent|em=1|1=Conventional MS and then [[fast atom bombardment]] MS enabled Williams to sequence biologically active peptides, including [[gastrin]] and [[insulin]].}}
*Determining the structures and modes of action of the [[vancomycin]] family of antibiotics
{{block indent|em=1|1=In 1969 Dudley took on the problem of determining the structure of vancomycin, a powerful natural antibiotic active against [[Gram-positive bacteria]].}}
*Evolution
{{block indent|em=1|1=Williams "argued powerfully that 'natural products' such as the alkaloids
found in many plant species that have no known function must have a vital but unknown role in order to justify the evolutionary effort and energy expenditure in maintaining their presence through many cycles of natural selection.<ref name=roysoc/><ref>{{cite journal|last1=Williams|first1=Dudley&nbsp;H.|last2=Stone|first2=Martin&nbsp;J.|last3=Hauck|first3=Peter&nbsp;R.|last4=Rahman|first4=Shirley&nbsp;K.|title=Why Are Secondary Metabolites (Natural Products) Biosynthesized?|journal=J. Nat. Prod.|volume=52|issue=6|date=1989|pages=1189–1208|doi=10.1021/np50066a001 |pmid=2693613 |bibcode=1989JNAtP..52.1189W }}</ref>}}

==Awards and honours==
*1964 Fellow of [[Churchill College, Cambridge|Churchill College]]
*1966 [[Meldola Medal and Prize|Meldola Medal]], Royal Institute of Chemistry
*1968 [[Corday–Morgan Prize|Corday–Morgan Medal]], The Chemical Society
*1983 [[Fellow of the Royal Society]]
*Tilden Medal, Royal Society of Chemistry
*1984 Structural Chemistry Award, Royal Society of Chemistry
*1990 [[Academia Europaea]]
*1990 [[Bader Award]], Royal Society of Chemistry
*1996 Leo Friend Award, American Chemical Society

==Personal life==
Dudley and Pat had two sons, Mark Howard in 1966 and Simon Bedford in 1968.
Williams retired in 2004. Six years later he was diagnosed with an aggressive carcinoma of the liver. He died in a hospice in Cambridge on 3 November 2010.<ref name=roysoc/>
